title: Disability & the Politics of Help
hook: Grabbing a wheelchair or a blind man's arm feels like kindness, and to the person on the receiving end it often feels like being moved like furniture.
why:
Most people who have not lived with disability have never been taught how to behave around it, and many of them feel it. In a 2014 survey for the disability charity Scope, about two-thirds of British adults said they felt uncomfortable talking to disabled people, most often because they were afraid of saying or doing the wrong thing. That discomfort shows in the body. People stare, or look carefully away. They talk to the companion instead. They lean on the wheelchair, grab an arm, or rush in to help with something the person was managing perfectly well.

For a disabled man, these small moments add up. Each one says, in the language of the body, that he is less capable than he is, or that his body and his equipment are open to anyone. For the man doing the helping, they are usually well meant, and that is exactly why they persist.

This chapter covers the politics of help: asking before acting, meeting someone at eye level, guiding a blind person properly, reading a face that cannot move, the conventions of Deaf space, the trap of assuming that one difference means many, and reading a different body against its own baseline.

teach.p:
The most common mistake non-disabled people make around disability is not hostility but help. In 2019 the psychologist Michelle Nario-Redmond and her colleagues described three forms of prejudice against disabled people. Hostile ableism includes bullying and abuse. Benevolent ableism treats disabled people as fragile, childlike or in need of rescue. Ambivalent ableism mixes the two. In accounts of what disabled people meet day to day, help that nobody asked for is among the experiences most often reported.

Unasked-for help is a nonverbal act. Someone takes hold of a wheelchair and starts pushing. Someone grabs the elbow of a blind man at a crossing and steers him across. Someone lifts a bag from a man walking with a cane. Each says, without words, that the helper has judged the situation and decided that the other person cannot manage it. It also takes away control: the person being helped may have been going somewhere else, at a different pace, by a different route.

The rule disability organisations teach is simple. Ask first: would you like a hand? Then wait for the answer, and accept it if it is no. If it is yes, ask how. A wheelchair user may want the door held but not the chair pushed. A blind man may want directions rather than an arm.

The figure here sits upright in a manual wheelchair, hands resting near the rims. The chair is how he moves, and he is in control of it. Treat it as part of his personal space, as you would treat his body: do not lean on it, hang a bag on it, or move it without asking.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if disabled people generally welcomed help given without asking. Accounts gathered by disability researchers and organisations consistently list unasked-for help among the most common and least welcome experiences.
teach.pullQuote: Ask first, then wait for the answer, and accept it if it is no.

teach.p:
A seated person's eyes are around 120 centimetres from the floor; a standing man's are typically 40 to 50 centimetres higher. In a passing exchange this hardly matters. In a longer conversation, standing close to someone in a wheelchair forces him to tip his head back and look up, which tires the neck, and it puts him in a position this book has described many times as lower status: looked down on, literally.

The fix is easy. For anything longer than a passing word, sit down if there is a chair, or step back far enough that the other person can see your face without craning. Crouching can work for a moment, but it can look like talking to a child, so a chair is usually better.

A second rule matters as much: talk to the person, not the companion. The habit of addressing a disabled person's partner, carer or friend instead of the disabled person himself is so common that a long-running BBC Radio 4 programme on disability took its name from it: Does He Take Sugar? Waiters ask the companion what he will order. Receptionists ask the companion to fill in his form. Direct your eyes, your questions and your body to the person himself, even if he uses an interpreter or a communication aid.

The figures here sit at the same height, facing each other. The standing man has pulled up a chair. Nothing about the conversation needs to change except the height of his eyes, and that one change turns it into a conversation between equals.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if height made no difference to how a conversation feels. Wheelchair users widely report that being stood over, and being bypassed in favour of a companion, are among the most diminishing parts of everyday encounters.

teach.p:
A long white cane tells others that its user is blind or has low vision. It does not tell them he needs help, and it is never an invitation to take his arm. Being grabbed and steered is disorienting: the blind person loses his own sense of where he is, may be pulled off his route, and may have no idea who has hold of him.

The technique taught by sight loss charities such as the RNIB is called sighted guiding. First, introduce yourself and ask whether he would like help. If he would, offer your elbow rather than taking his. He holds your arm just above the elbow and walks half a step behind, which lets him feel through your arm when you turn, stop, step up or step down. Walk at his pace, and say what is coming: a kerb, steps going up, a narrow doorway. For a narrow gap, move your guiding arm behind your back to signal that he should step in behind you.

A few other habits help. Say your name when you approach, since he may not recognise your voice. Say when you are leaving, so that he is not left talking to empty air. Do not pet, feed or distract a guide dog in harness; it is working. And give directions in words that do not depend on sight: about ten steps ahead, on your left, rather than over there.

The figure here walks with his cane sweeping ahead, head level, his free arm relaxed. He is not lost. He is travelling the way he has learned to travel, and the most useful thing a stranger can do is keep out of the cane's path, or ask.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if grabbing a blind person's arm were as effective and welcome as offering an elbow. Sight loss charities teach the offered elbow precisely because it leaves the blind person in control and lets him read movement through your arm.

teach.p:
Much of this book has been about reading faces. Some faces cannot be read in the usual way. Facial paralysis can follow a stroke, Bell's palsy, surgery or injury, and some people are born with it, as in Moebius syndrome, a rare condition that leaves the face largely unable to move. A man with Moebius syndrome may feel delight, amusement or grief as fully as anyone, but none of it reaches the muscles that smile or frown.

The psychologist Kathleen Bogart, who herself has Moebius syndrome, has studied how others respond. In a 2014 study with Linda Tickle-Degnen and Nalini Ambady, observers watched or listened to people with facial paralysis describing happy and sad experiences. People with more severe paralysis were rated as less happy than people with milder paralysis, whichever combination of face, voice and body the observers were given. The still face was read as a flat mood.

Bogart's work also points to a remedy. People with facial paralysis, especially those born with it, often express emotion through other channels: the voice, gesture, posture, the timing of laughter. In 2015 Bogart and Tickle-Degnen reported that a brief training, which encouraged observers to attend to those channels rather than the face, improved their impressions. The lesson reaches beyond paralysis. When a face is still, because of a condition, medication, a culture of restraint or simple temperament, listen to the voice and watch the hands before deciding what someone feels.

The figure here stands with a neutral face and a level gaze. Without his voice and the context, nothing in that face tells you whether he is content, bored or moved, and that is the point: a still face is the absence of a signal, not a signal of absence.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if observers read the emotions of people with facial paralysis as accurately as anyone else's. Bogart and colleagues found that severe paralysis led observers to see less happiness than the speakers were describing.
teach.pullQuote: A still face is the absence of a signal, not a signal of absence.

teach.p:
Deaf people who use a sign language, such as British Sign Language or American Sign Language, share a culture with its own nonverbal conventions, and several of them reverse hearing habits. Many write Deaf with a capital D to mark that cultural identity, as distinct from the medical fact of hearing loss.

Getting attention is the first difference. Calling a name across the room does nothing. Instead, Deaf people wave within the other person's line of sight, tap a shoulder or arm lightly, stamp on a wooden floor so that the vibration carries, or flick the lights to get a group's attention. To a hearing person, a tap on the shoulder from a near stranger can feel intrusive; in Deaf company it is ordinary manners.

Eye contact is the second. A signed conversation is visual, so the person watching must keep looking. Looking away while someone signs is like covering your ears while they speak, and it can end the conversation. Hearing people raised to soften their gaze may find the steadiness intense; it is simply how the language works.

The third is the face. In sign languages, facial expressions do grammatical work: raised eyebrows can mark a yes-or-no question, furrowed brows a question asking who, what or where, and mouth shapes can change what a sign means. An expressive face on a Deaf signer is often grammar, not emotion, and reading it as anger or drama is a mistake.

For someone who lip-reads, face him, keep your hands and food away from your mouth, do not shout or exaggerate, and stand where the light falls on your face. Only part of speech is visible on the lips, so lip-reading is tiring and partial. The figure here waves, which in Deaf company is the polite way to say: I would like to talk to you.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if Deaf signers used attention-getting, eye contact and facial expression in the same way hearing speakers do. Sign language research and Deaf community guidance describe them as different, and in some respects opposite.

teach.p:
In her 1960 book Physical Disability: A Psychological Approach, the psychologist Beatrice Wright described a pattern she called spread: the tendency to assume that a disability in one area affects many others. Spread is why people raise their voices to a blind man, as if he were also deaf. It is why they speak slowly and simply to a wheelchair user, as if his legs and his mind were connected. It is why a man with a speech impairment is assumed to have an intellectual one.

Spread also works through the body. A slow, careful gait, a cane, a tremor or a stiff posture can be read as weakness of mind or mood, when it says nothing about either. A man who walks with a cane after a hip operation is the same man he was before it. The figure here walks with a cane, head up, at his own pace. Nothing about the pace of his feet tells you the pace of his thinking.

Not every disability is visible. Many people live with chronic pain, fatigue, epilepsy, heart conditions, mental illness or hearing loss that nobody can see. A man who takes the lift for one floor, sits in a priority seat or leaves a party early may be managing something invisible. In the United Kingdom and increasingly elsewhere, a lanyard printed with sunflowers, introduced at Gatwick Airport in 2016, is recognised as a discreet signal that the wearer has a hidden disability and may need extra time, space or help.

The working rule is to assume nothing beyond what you know. A disability tells you about one thing. Let the person tell you about everything else.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if a visible disability reliably predicted other impairments. Spread, as Wright described it, is an error of perception, and disabled people report meeting it constantly: being shouted at, talked down to and spoken about in the third person.

teach.p:
Earlier chapters have stressed reading against a baseline: noticing change in a person rather than comparing him with a general norm. Disability makes this rule essential. A man with Parkinson's disease may have a tremor, a soft voice and a face that moves less than it did, none of which signals nerves or lack of interest. A man with cerebral palsy may have movements that look tense or abrupt. A man recovering from a brain injury may speak slowly or flatly. Someone with a chronic pain condition may shift, wince or stand up often, which is not impatience.

Read each of these against the person's own pattern. Once you know how someone usually moves and sounds, changes become meaningful again: a man whose tremor is worse than usual may be tired, stressed or unwell, and a wheelchair user who has stopped joining in may be shut out by the layout of the room rather than uninterested.

Asking is allowed. Disabled people differ in how much they want to talk about their bodies, but most prefer a direct, respectful question to silent guessing or staring. Is there anything that would make this easier? is usually welcome. Questions from strangers about how someone became disabled usually are not.

Finally, notice the room. Much of what looks like a person's limitation is a limitation of the space: steps, narrow aisles, loud rooms, dim light, tables at the wrong height. The figure here listens, leaning slightly forward, his attention on the other person, the posture of someone trying to learn how this particular person works rather than assuming.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the usual cues of emotion and attention applied unchanged to people with different bodies. Tremor, reduced facial movement and unusual movement are features of many conditions, and say nothing by themselves about mood or interest.

poseGallery.annotation: For a conversation of more than a minute, sit down or step back. He should not have to crane to see your face.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Moving in to help without asking
poseGallery.annotation: Unasked-for help takes away control. Ask whether he would like a hand, and accept no as an answer.
In a signed conversation, looking away is like covering your ears. Keep your eyes on the signer.

poseGallery.doCaption: His own route, with an elbow offered if he wants it
poseGallery.dontCaption: Steering a blind man by the arm
poseGallery.annotation: Being grabbed and steered is disorienting. Introduce yourself, ask, and offer your elbow rather than taking his.
For someone who lip-reads, a turned head ends the conversation. Face the person, and keep your mouth in view.

caseStudy:
Ravi, thirty-nine, became a wheelchair user after a cycling accident three years ago. He works as an engineer, plays wheelchair basketball on Thursdays and has a dry sense of humour about most things. What wears him down, he says, is not the chair but the way people behave around it.

Strangers take hold of his handles to push him up ramps he was managing. Waiters ask his wife what he would like. At work events, colleagues stand in a tight circle above him, and he spends the evening looking at belt buckles or straining his neck until he gives up and leaves early. Once, in a shop, a man patted him on the shoulder and told him he was an inspiration for being out.

His brother-in-law, Paul, a kind man who had never known anyone disabled, admitted that he had done several of these things in the first year. At a family wedding he had pushed Ravi across the lawn without asking, because the grass looked difficult, and had been hurt when Ravi snapped at him. Ravi's sister explained it later: it was like someone grabbing your arm and steering you across a room.

Paul changed a few habits. He asks before he helps, and when Ravi says no, he leaves it. At family gatherings he pulls up a chair rather than standing over him, and he has noticed that others start sitting down too. When a waiter turned to him to ask what Ravi wanted, he simply looked at Ravi and waited.

Ravi says the difference is not that Paul is careful around him now. It is that Paul has stopped being careful around him, and started treating him as the same man he was before, who happens to sit down.
observe: Notice, the next time you see a wheelchair user in conversation, the heights of everyone's eyes and who is looking up.
Notice whom staff address when a disabled person is with a companion: the person, or the companion.
Notice any impulse you have to help a disabled stranger, and whether you would ask first.
Notice a space you use every day, such as your office or a favourite café, and where steps, narrow gaps, noise or lighting would make it hard to use.

drills.name: Ask, Wait, Accept
steps: Think of three situations where you might offer help to a disabled person: a door, a ramp, a crossing.
For each, write the words you would use to offer help.
Write what you will do if the answer is no.
Practise saying the offer aloud until it sounds natural rather than anxious.
variations: Practise your offer of help in three different settings, a station, a shop and an office, and notice how the words change.
Ask a disabled friend or colleague how they prefer to be offered help, and whether there are offers they find tiring.
Notice the next time someone offers you help you do not need, and how it feels to say no.

drills.name: Learn Sighted Guiding
steps: Watch a demonstration of sighted guiding from a sight loss charity.
With a willing friend, practise offering your elbow while he walks with his eyes closed.
Walk a short route that includes a doorway, a step and a narrow gap.
Swap roles, and notice what it feels like to be guided well, and to be pulled.
Note one thing you would do differently with a stranger.
variations: Learn how to guide someone through a doorway, onto an escalator and into a seat, using a sight loss charity's guidance.
Practise describing a room to a friend with their eyes closed, telling them where the door, the chairs and the table are.
Notice whether the places you use often have tactile paving, audio announcements and clear signage, and where they do not.

drills.name: Eye-Level Audit
steps: At your next meeting or social event, notice who is sitting and who is standing.
Sit down for one conversation with a seated person you would normally stand over.
Notice how the conversation changes in length and tone.
variations: At your next event, count how many seated people are being spoken to by standing people, and whether anyone sits down to join them.
Move a chair into a conversation with a seated person, and notice how many others follow your lead.
In a meeting, check that everyone can see everyone else's face, including anyone who lip-reads or uses a wheelchair.

drills.name: Spread Check
steps: Think of a disabled person you know or have met.
List any assumptions you made about him beyond what his disability actually involves.
Ask what evidence you had for each one.
Write one sentence about what you will assume next time, which is nothing extra.
variations: Notice an assumption you have made about someone with an invisible disability, and what evidence you had.
Notice how often people speak more slowly or loudly to someone with a visible disability, and whether that person seems to need it.
Write down what you know about a disabled person's abilities beyond their disability, and notice whether you had assumed any limits.

quiz.q: A colleague says that when you see a wheelchair user on a ramp, the kind thing is to start pushing, since he can always say if he minds. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since most wheelchair users welcome a push and will say so if they mind it
Ask first and wait for an answer, since unasked-for help takes away the person's control
Never offer help at all, since any offer of help is an insult to a disabled person
Push only on the steepest ramps, since gentle ramps are easy enough for anyone to manage
quiz.explain: Unasked-for help is among the experiences disabled people most often report as unwelcome. Asking first, and accepting no, leaves the person in control of his own body and chair.

quiz.q: What did Bogart, Tickle-Degnen and Ambady find in their 2014 study of facial paralysis?
options: People with severe paralysis were rated as less happy than people with milder paralysis
Observers read the emotions of people with paralysis as accurately as anyone else's
Observers relied on the face alone and ignored the voice and body completely in every case
People with facial paralysis were rated as happier than others, because they seemed calm
quiz.explain: Observers rated people with severe paralysis as less happy, whichever combination of face, voice and body they were given. A still face was read as a flat mood.

quiz.q: In a conversation in sign language, what does looking away from the signer usually do?
options: It shows respect, as it does in the many hearing cultures that soften their eye contact
It has no effect at all, since the signer will simply carry on until you look back again
It is like covering your ears while someone speaks, and it can end the conversation
It signals that you have understood the point and are ready for the signer to move on
quiz.explain: A signed conversation is visual, so the person watching has to keep looking. Breaking eye contact cuts off the language itself, not just a social signal.

quiz.q: What did Beatrice Wright mean by spread?
options: The way a disability gradually spreads to other parts of the body as time goes on
The tendency to assume that a disability in one area affects many others as well
The spread of disability rights laws from one country to many others since the 1990s
The way that disabled people spread their weight differently in order to stay balanced
quiz.explain: Spread is the error of assuming that one disability implies others, such as shouting at a blind man or talking down to a wheelchair user. It is a mistake in the perceiver, not a feature of the disability.

quiz.q: A blind man with a long cane is standing at a busy crossing. What fits this chapter best?
options: Take his arm firmly and walk him across, since the traffic is fast and dangerous
Say nothing at all, since offering help to a blind man is always unwelcome to him
Call out directions to him from across the street as soon as the lights change
Introduce yourself, ask if he would like help, and offer your elbow if he would
quiz.explain: Sighted guiding starts with an introduction and a question. If he accepts, offering your elbow lets him hold on and feel your movements, leaving him in control.

quiz.q: At a work event, a waiter asks you what your colleague, who uses a wheelchair, would like to drink. What fits this chapter best?
options: Answer for him, since you know what he usually drinks and it saves everyone some time
Look at your colleague and wait, so that the waiter turns to him and asks him directly
Tell the waiter off loudly, so that everyone can see how rude he was to your colleague
Go and fetch the drink yourself, so that nobody else has to deal with the situation
quiz.explain: Talking to the companion instead of the disabled person is so common that a BBC programme on disability was named after it. Turning your eyes to him redirects the waiter without embarrassing anyone.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of what Nario-Redmond and colleagues called benevolent ableism?
options: Openly bullying a disabled colleague and making fun of how they move
Treating a disabled person as fragile or in need of rescue, such as pushing without asking
Building a ramp into a public building so that wheelchair users can enter it
Refusing to hire a disabled candidate because of an unwillingness to make any reasonable adjustments
quiz.explain: Benevolent ableism treats disabled people as fragile, childlike or in need of rescue. Unasked-for help, such as pushing a wheelchair without asking, is a common example, kind in intention and patronising in effect.

quiz.q: At a bank counter, a Deaf customer has typed her problem on her phone. What fits this chapter best for the cashier?
options: Speak very slowly and loudly, exaggerating each word so that she can lip-read it more easily
Face her, keep the mouth visible, write things down and let her lead on how to communicate
Ask the hearing customer behind her to explain what she wants, since he can hear
Turn to the screen while speaking, so that the problem can be sorted out more quickly
quiz.explain: Exaggerated or shouted speech is harder to lip-read, turning away hides the mouth, and speaking through a hearing stranger is a form of spread. Facing her, writing and letting her lead respects her as the customer.

quiz.q: Someone says that a person using a priority seat who does not look disabled is probably taking advantage. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That many disabilities are invisible, so assume they have a reason, as you would want them to of you
That anyone using a priority seat should be asked to prove their disability to the other passengers
That priority seats are only for people using wheelchairs, canes or guide dogs, and nobody else
That younger people are rarely disabled, so they should give up priority seats when asked
quiz.explain: Chronic pain, fatigue, heart conditions, epilepsy and many other disabilities do not show. Assuming that an ordinary-looking body is fully able is spread in reverse.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific encounter with a disabled person, as a stranger, colleague, friend or relative, or a time when you were treated differently because of a disability or injury of your own. Describe what bodies did: who stood and who sat, who was addressed, who helped, and whether anyone asked first. What did the person on the receiving end seem to feel? If you could replay the moment, what would you do differently with your eyes, your hands or your position in the room?
reflection.guidance: Many people feel embarrassed recalling these moments, since most of the mistakes were made with good intentions. That is the point of the exercise. Focus on concrete behaviour, such as height, gaze and touch, rather than on whether you were a good person, and include any time you were on the receiving end, even with a temporary injury.

failureMode: The first failure is to help without asking, taking hold of a chair, an arm or a bag, which removes the other person's control however kindly it is meant. The second is to stand over a seated person through a long conversation, or to address the companion instead of the person. The third is to grab a blind man rather than offer an elbow, or to walk away without saying so. The fourth is to read a still face as a still mood, when paralysis, medication or temperament may hide what someone feels. The fifth is to bring hearing habits into Deaf space: calling out, looking away while someone signs, reading grammatical expressions as emotion. And the sixth is spread: assuming that a disability in one area means others, and talking down to a man whose mind is untouched.

moreCases.title: The father at the engagement party
moreCases.scene:
Geoff, sixty-four, was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease five years ago. His tremor is mostly controlled by medication, but his face moves much less than it used to, his voice has become soft and flat, and he moves slowly, especially when he is tired. His son, Tom, is engaged to Priya, and her parents are hosting an engagement party at their home. It is the first time Geoff and his wife, Linda, have met them.

Priya's father, Raj, greets Geoff warmly and talks to him about the wedding plans. Geoff listens, nods slightly and answers in a quiet monotone. His face barely changes. When Raj makes a joke about the cost of the wedding, Geoff's expression stays still. When Priya's mother shows them the garden she has spent twenty years on, Geoff says "Very nice" in the same level voice.

After an hour, Raj says quietly to his wife that Tom's father does not seem very happy about the engagement. Priya's mother agrees that he seemed cold. Priya, overhearing, is upset, and asks Tom whether his dad has a problem with her family.

Tom is horrified. He tells Priya that his father has been talking about the engagement for weeks, that he cried when Tom told him, and that he had told Tom in the car on the way there how much he liked her parents' house.

Geoff had also taken his medication late that afternoon, because the drive had run on, and he knows that his face and voice are flatter when the timing slips. He had not thought to mention it.

Linda, watching from across the room, can see that Geoff is tired, and wishes she had found a way to tell Priya's parents earlier. She has done it so many times that she had hoped, this once, she would not need to.
moreCases.misread:
Raj and his wife read Geoff's still face, soft monotone and slow responses as coldness and disapproval of the engagement. They read him against the general expectation of how a happy father looks, not against his own baseline.

Priya, hearing her parents, read the coldness as a judgment on her family, which turned a misunderstanding about a face into a worry about a marriage.

Geoff, for his part, had no idea how he was coming across. Inside, he was enjoying himself more than he had in months, and he assumed it showed.

Raj's wife also read Geoff's slow movements, as he got up from the sofa, as reluctance to join the tour of the garden, when it was simply how long it took him to stand.
moreCases.betterRead:
Parkinson's can reduce facial expression and flatten the voice, so that feelings which are fully present do not reach the face. Bogart, Tickle-Degnen and Ambady found that people with more severe facial paralysis were rated as less happy than people with milder paralysis, whatever they were actually describing: observers read a still face as a still mood. This chapter's rule is to read each person against his own pattern. Geoff's still face was simply his face now. The better response, which Tom and Linda made the same evening, was to explain, briefly and without fuss, that Geoff has Parkinson's, which affects his expression and voice, and that he was delighted. Raj sat down beside Geoff, asked him about his own wedding and listened to the words rather than watching the face. Geoff talked for half an hour. Raj said later that it was the best conversation of the party.

Linda also suggested that, for big family occasions, Geoff take his medication on time and rest beforehand, which made a visible difference at the wedding itself.

moreCases.title: The traveller at the station
moreCases.scene:
Abdul, forty-five, has been blind since his twenties and travels to work by train every day with a long white cane. One morning his usual platform is changed at short notice because of engineering works. The announcement is muffled, and the information screens he cannot see are the only clear source. He stops near the top of the stairs to listen for another announcement.

A man in a hurry sees him, says "Here, let me help you, mate," takes hold of his upper arm and starts steering him briskly down the stairs to platform three. Abdul, caught off balance, says that he is not sure he needs platform three, but the man is already moving. At the bottom, the man lets go, says "There you go," and is gone. Abdul does not know which platform he is on, which way he is facing, or where the stairs are.

A woman who saw it happen comes over. She says, "Hello, I'm Joanna. Would you like some help finding your train?" Abdul says yes, he is trying to get the 8.12 to Leeds. She checks the screen, tells him it has moved to platform five, and asks whether he would like to take her arm. He says yes. She offers her elbow, and he takes it just above the joint.

As they walk, she tells him when the stairs are coming, whether they go up or down, and when there is a gap in the crowd.

Abdul has had this happen before, more times than he can count. He has learned to say "Please don't take my arm" quickly, but on this morning the man was moving before he could speak.

He has been travelling this route for twelve years, and he knows the station well. What he needs on a morning like this is information, not an escort.
moreCases.misread:
The first man read a blind man pausing at the top of the stairs as a man in need of rescue, and read his own grip on Abdul's arm as kindness. He took Abdul's control of his own movement without asking where he wanted to go.

He also read Abdul's protest as polite reluctance to accept help, rather than as a man telling him he was going the wrong way.

The other commuters, watching the man march Abdul down the stairs, read it as a kind stranger helping, and only Joanna saw that Abdul had been taken somewhere he had not asked to go.
moreCases.betterRead:
Nario-Redmond and colleagues described benevolent ableism as treating disabled people as fragile or in need of rescue, and unasked-for help is among the experiences disabled people report most often. Being grabbed and steered is disorienting: Abdul lost his sense of where he was and was left on the wrong platform. Joanna did what sight loss charities such as the RNIB teach: she introduced herself, asked whether he wanted help, asked where he was going, offered her elbow rather than taking his, walked at his pace and described what was coming. At platform five, she told him where he was standing, which way the train would come from and where the nearest bench was, and said goodbye so that he knew she was leaving. Abdul caught his train. He said later that the difference between the two helpers was the difference between being moved and being accompanied.

Abdul also asked the station staff to make sure platform changes were announced clearly twice, which they now do.

Joanna, for her part, said it was the first time she had used the technique she had learned from a charity leaflet, and that it was far easier than she had expected.

moreCases.title: The customer at the bank counter
moreCases.scene:
Ellen, thirty-three, is Deaf and uses British Sign Language. She goes into her bank to sort out a problem with a payment that has been taken twice. There is a queue. When her turn comes, the cashier calls "Next, please!" and Ellen, who is reading a leaflet, does not respond. The cashier calls again, louder, and the man behind Ellen taps her on the shoulder and points.

At the counter, Ellen signs that she is Deaf and points to her ear, then takes out her phone, where she has typed a note explaining the problem. The cashier, flustered, begins to speak very slowly and loudly, exaggerating every word, and then turns to her screen while still talking, so that Ellen can no longer see her mouth. When she turns back, she asks Ellen a question in the same exaggerated way, and Ellen cannot follow it. Ellen types a reply. The cashier reads it and says, to the man behind Ellen, "I think she wants a refund."

Ellen feels her face go hot. She has been talked about, in the third person, in front of a queue, to a stranger.

The branch manager, Gareth, has seen it from his desk. He comes over, smiles at Ellen, picks up a notepad and writes, "I'm the manager. Shall we sort this out at my desk?"

The man behind her, it turns out, also looked away rather than at Ellen when the cashier spoke to him, embarrassed, as if he too were unsure who the conversation belonged to.

She has used this branch for six years. In that time, nobody behind the counter has learned to wave rather than call her name.
moreCases.misread:
The cashier read Ellen's deafness as a barrier to be overcome by volume and exaggeration, and when that failed, turned to the hearing man behind her as if he were Ellen's spokesman. She brought hearing habits into an exchange where they did not work.

The man behind her read the shoulder tap he gave her as helping, which it was, and then read the cashier's question to him as his to answer, which it was not.

The cashier, if asked, would have said she was trying her best, which was true. Her best was built on habits that suited hearing customers and failed Ellen.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter describes how Deaf space reverses several hearing habits: calling out does nothing, faces must stay visible, and the person you are talking to is the person in front of you. Exaggerated, slow speech is harder to lip-read, not easier, and turning to a screen hides the mouth. Speaking to the man behind her was a version of spread, treating Ellen as unable to speak for herself. Gareth's better approach was simple. He wrote, faced her when he did speak, kept his mouth visible and let her lead on how they would communicate. At his desk, they exchanged written notes for ten minutes and resolved the double payment. He also asked her whether the bank could do anything better. She suggested that staff learn to wave or tap the counter to get a Deaf customer's attention and keep a notepad at every till. Gareth arranged both.

Ellen also wrote to the bank's head office, with Gareth's encouragement, and the notepads appeared at every branch in the region.

Gareth also learned to sign "hello" and "thank you", which Ellen said, when she next came in, made her laugh and made her day.

moreCases.title: The engineer who stammered
moreCases.scene:
Imran, thirty, is a civil engineer, and he has a stammer. On some words, especially at the start of a sentence or under pressure, his speech blocks: his mouth forms the first sound and nothing comes for several seconds, or a sound repeats. He knows exactly what he wants to say. In meetings, this is when the trouble starts.

When Imran blocks, his colleagues react in a few predictable ways. Some look away, out of kindness, which leaves him talking to the side of their heads. Some finish his sentence for him, usually wrongly. One manager, Clive, has a habit of saying "Take your time" in a tone that makes Imran feel like a child, and then moving on to someone else before Imran has finished. In one design review, a visiting client began to address his questions to Imran's junior colleague, as if Imran were not the lead engineer.

Imran has started to say less in meetings. He emails his views afterwards instead. His annual review notes that he "lacks presence in meetings" and "could be more assertive".

His new manager, Gemma, reads the review and asks Imran what would help. He tells her: wait, keep looking at me, do not finish my words, and do not move on until I have finished.

At home, with friends and family, Imran stammers much less, and he has noticed that the meetings where people look away and hurry him are the meetings where it is worst.

He has also noticed that the client who turned to his junior colleague did not do so on the second day of the review, after Imran presented the structural calculations without a single block.

His previous manager, he later learned, had written the comment about presence after a single meeting in which Imran had blocked badly while presenting to the board.
moreCases.misread:
His colleagues read Imran's blocks as difficulty in thinking or a lack of confidence, and responded by looking away, finishing his sentences or moving on. The client read his stammer as a sign that someone else must be in charge, which is spread at work.

And the review read the consequences of those reactions, his silence and his emails, as a personality trait.

Imran also read his colleagues' looking away as embarrassment on his behalf, which made each block feel more shameful than the last.

Clive's "take your time", meant as patience, was read by everyone else in the room as a signal that Imran was struggling, which made the next block more likely.
moreCases.betterRead:
Beatrice Wright described spread as the assumption that a disability in one area affects others, and a stammer is often mistaken for a lack of intelligence, confidence or authority. Part I's chapter on the voice touched on stammering, and the advice of stammering organisations is consistent: wait, keep natural eye contact, do not finish words and do not hurry the speaker. Imran's blocks were a feature of his speech, not his mind, and the review had turned the effect of others' reactions into a judgment of him. Gemma's better approach was to do what Imran asked and to make it the norm. She told the team, with his agreement, how they could help, and in meetings she waited, kept her eyes on him and did not move on until he had finished. She also removed the comment about presence from his review. Imran began speaking in meetings again, and led the next client review.

Clive, when Gemma explained, said he had thought he was being kind, and asked Imran directly what he should do instead.

workedReading.title: Hosting a wheelchair user for dinner
workedReading.scene:
Matthew, thirty-six, has invited a new colleague, Lucy, thirty-four, and her husband, Sam, to dinner at his flat with a few friends. Lucy is a wheelchair user after a spinal injury in her twenties. She is funny, sharp and a keen cook, and Matthew wants her to enjoy the evening as much as anyone else. He has never had a guest who uses a wheelchair, and he realises, as he plans, that his flat is on the first floor and that he does not know whether she can get in. He also knows from this chapter that the biggest risks are not hostility but helpfulness: grabbing, steering, standing over and talking to the companion. He decides to ask rather than guess, and to treat Lucy as a guest first and a wheelchair user second.

He also remembers a work party at which he saw a wheelchair user spend the whole evening looking up at a circle of standing colleagues, and leave early. He wants his evening to be different.

He also asks Sam, privately, whether there is anything he should know, and Sam says only that Lucy hates being fussed over, which Matthew takes as the most useful advice of all.

steps.label: Ask about access first
steps.text:
He messages Lucy a week before: "My flat's on the first floor and there's a lift, but the front door has a step. Is that manageable, or would you prefer we went to a restaurant? Anything else that would help?" Lucy replies that a single step is fine with her chair, that she would rather come to his flat, and that the main thing is space to turn in the bathroom. She thanks him for asking. Most people, she says, do not.

He also asks whether she would prefer any particular seat at the table, and she says somewhere she can get in and out without everyone having to move.

He also mentions where he lives and how to park nearby, which saves her a call to ask.

steps.label: Plan the room
steps.text:
He checks the bathroom and moves a laundry basket so that there is room to turn. He rearranges the living room so that there is a clear route from the door to the table, and moves the coffee table out of the way. He thinks about where everyone will sit, and plans for the pre-dinner drinks to happen around the sofa and armchairs, so that everyone is seated at the same level, rather than standing in a circle in the kitchen.

He also checks that the light switches and the door handle to the bathroom are within reach from a seated position, and leaves a lamp on in the hallway.

steps.label: Greet at eye level
steps.text:
When Lucy and Sam arrive, Matthew opens the door, greets Lucy first, by name, and steps back so that she can come in at her own pace. He does not take hold of her chair to help her over the step; she manages it with a quick tilt. In the living room, he sits down to talk to her rather than standing over her. As this chapter describes, sitting puts their eyes at the same height and spares her neck.

He also greets Sam, but second, so that the order of the greeting tells everyone who the guest is.

He also offers to take her coat, as he would anyone's, and hangs it where she can reach it herself when she leaves.

steps.label: Let her lead on help
steps.text:
At one point Lucy reaches for a bowl of crisps on a high shelf in the kitchen. Matthew's instinct is to grab it for her. He stops and asks, "Would you like me to get that?" She says, "No, I've got it," and uses a long-handled grabber from her bag. He says nothing more. Asking, waiting and accepting the answer, as the Ask, Wait, Accept drill rehearses, means that help stays her decision.

Later, when she does ask him to pass something from across the table, he passes it, as he would for anyone. Asking works in both directions.

He also notices how strong the urge to help was, and how little it had to do with anything Lucy needed.

steps.label: Talk to her, not her husband
steps.text:
When one of Matthew's friends, meeting Lucy for the first time, asks Sam whether Lucy would like a drink, Matthew turns to Lucy and waits, so that the question goes to her. Lucy says, cheerfully, "A gin, please, and I can answer for myself, but thanks, Sam's quite used to it." Everyone laughs, including the friend, who goes red and then asks Lucy about her work.

He also notices that the friend, after going red, treats Lucy no differently for the rest of the evening, which is exactly the right recovery.

He also notices that the friend's mistake was the same one the waiter made with Ravi, and that it happens even among kind people.

steps.label: Keep the evening ordinary
steps.text:
Over dinner, the conversation is about cooking, work, holidays and a film everyone has seen. Nobody asks Lucy what happened to her, and nobody tells her she is an inspiration. When she offers to help with the washing up, Matthew says yes, as he would to anyone, and lowers the drying rack onto the table so that she can reach it.

He also notices that the evening's best conversation is between Lucy and a friend who is a chef, about bread, and that disability does not come up once.

He also makes sure the dessert is served at the table rather than on a high kitchen counter, so that everyone helps themselves at the same height.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
At the end of the evening, Lucy says it was the most relaxed dinner she had been to in months, and asks Matthew to come to hers next time so that she can show off her cooking. Sam tells Matthew quietly that the message about access had made Lucy decide to come. Matthew writes down what he learned: ask first, plan the room, sit down, ask before helping, let her answer for herself, and then forget about it.

He also realises that most of the planning took ten minutes, and that the hardest part was resisting the urge to help.

moreFailures.title: Calling someone an inspiration for ordinary things
moreFailures.body:
Telling a disabled person that they are an inspiration for going shopping, catching a train, going to work or being out at all is usually meant as praise. To many disabled people it lands as a reminder that others expected them to be at home, and that ordinary life is seen as remarkable when they do it. The man who patted Ravi on the shoulder in the shop was expressing admiration; what Ravi heard was that a wheelchair user buying milk was surprising. Nario-Redmond and colleagues describe this kind of praise as part of benevolent ableism: it is kind in intention and patronising in effect. If a disabled person does something genuinely remarkable, such as winning a race or building a company, say so, as you would to anyone. For ordinary life, the respectful response is the ordinary one: nothing at all.

If you feel admiration, ask yourself whether you would feel it for a non-disabled person doing the same thing. If not, keep it to yourself.

moreFailures.title: Asking what happened
moreFailures.body:
"What happened to you?" and "Were you born like that?" are among the first questions many disabled people are asked by strangers, sometimes before their name. The curiosity is natural, but the question puts the person's body and history at the centre of a meeting with someone they do not know, and asks them to explain it on demand. Many disabled people describe being asked it several times a week. Some are happy to talk about their disability with people they know well; few want to with a stranger at a bus stop or a colleague on their first day. If someone wants you to know, they will tell you. Until then, ask about the things you would ask anyone: their work, their weekend, the film they saw. Lucy's evening went well partly because nobody asked.

If you are curious, notice that the question is about your curiosity, not their needs, and let it go.

If a disabled colleague does tell you about their condition, listen, and follow their lead on how much to discuss it.

moreFailures.title: Moving someone's mobility aids
moreFailures.body:
A wheelchair, a cane, a walking frame or a guide dog's harness is, for many people, part of how they move through the world, and moving it can feel much like being moved. Pushing a wheelchair without asking is the obvious example, but there are others: moving a cane that is leaning against a table so that someone can sit down, folding a walker out of the way, hanging a bag on a wheelchair's handles, leaning on the chair while talking, or distracting a working guide dog. Each takes away something the person relies on, or touches their personal space without permission. Leave mobility aids where their owners put them. If one is genuinely in the way, ask the person before touching it. And never move one out of reach of someone who needs it to get up.

If you have moved one by mistake, put it back within reach at once and say so.

moreFailures.title: Doubting disabilities you cannot see
moreFailures.body:
Many disabilities are not visible: chronic pain, fatigue conditions, heart and lung conditions, epilepsy, autism, mental illness, hearing loss and many others. People with them often use accessible toilets, priority seats, blue badges and lifts, and are sometimes challenged, glared at or told that they do not look disabled. That reading is spread in reverse: assuming that a body that looks ordinary must be fully able. It can be humiliating and, for someone who is struggling to stand on a crowded train, harmful. If someone is using an accessible facility or a priority seat, assume they have a reason, as you would want them to assume of you. If you are a member of staff, follow your organisation's policy, which should not require people to prove or explain a disability in public.

If you are tempted to challenge someone, remember that the cost of being wrong falls entirely on them.

questions.q: Should I offer help to a disabled stranger?
questions.a:
You can offer, in the same way you would offer help to anyone who looked as though they might need it, and then follow their answer. Ask first, in an ordinary voice: "Would you like a hand with that?" Then wait, and accept the reply. If the answer is no, leave it, without insisting or looking hurt, as Paul learned to do with Ravi. If the answer is yes, ask how they would like you to help, because people often have a particular way of doing things that works for them, as Joanna asked Abdul. Never take hold of a person, their wheelchair, their cane or their bag without asking. Nario-Redmond and colleagues found that unasked-for help is among the experiences disabled people report most often, and the asking is what turns it into respect.

And if you are not sure whether someone wants help, it is fine to stay nearby without doing anything. Being available is not the same as intervening.

questions.q: What words should I use about disability?
questions.a:
Follow the person's own lead. Some people prefer to be called disabled people, and some prefer people with disabilities. Many Deaf people use a capital D to mark their culture, and many autistic people prefer "autistic person". If you are unsure, listen to how someone describes themselves, or ask. Some phrases are widely disliked: "confined to a wheelchair" or "wheelchair-bound", when the chair is what lets someone move; "suffers from", which assumes misery; "brave" or "inspirational" for ordinary life. "Wheelchair user", "blind", "Deaf" and "has a stammer" are generally fine. Above all, remember that words matter less than how you behave: talking to the person, asking before helping and treating them as the same as anyone else.

If you get a word wrong and someone corrects you, thank them and use their word. That is all that is needed.

It is also worth noticing that many disabled people are tired of debates about language and would rather people simply got the behaviour right.

questions.q: How should I talk to someone with a stammer or a speech impairment?
questions.a:
Wait, keep natural eye contact and let them finish. Do not finish their words or sentences for them, even when you think you know what is coming, because you are often wrong and it takes their speech away from them. Do not tell them to slow down, take a breath or relax, which most people with a stammer find unhelpful. Do not move on to someone else before they have finished, as Clive did with Imran. Keep your face relaxed and attentive, as you would with anyone who was speaking. If you genuinely did not understand something, it is fine to say so and ask them to repeat it, or to check what you heard. Above all, listen to what they are saying, which is what they want from you, rather than to how they are saying it.

In meetings, a chair who makes waiting the norm helps far more than any individual reassurance.

It also helps to give the person time in meetings, for example by asking for their view and then waiting, rather than calling on them for a quick answer.

questions.q: How can I get a Deaf person's attention and talk with them?
questions.a:
Wave within their line of sight, tap them lightly on the shoulder or arm, or, in a group, flick the lights, rather than calling out. When you speak, face them, keep your mouth visible and speak at a normal pace and volume; exaggerated, slow or shouted speech is harder to lip-read, not easier. Do not turn away to a screen or a document while speaking. Have a notepad or phone ready to write things down, and let the Deaf person lead on how you communicate, as Gareth did at the bank. If an interpreter is present, look at and speak to the Deaf person, not the interpreter. Do not look away while someone is signing, which is like walking out of a conversation. And never address a Deaf person through a hearing companion as if they were not there.

Learning a few signs, such as hello and thank you, is a small gesture many Deaf people appreciate, though it is no substitute for an interpreter in important conversations.

questions.q: What if I make a mistake?
questions.a:
Apologise briefly, correct it and move on, as Matthew's friend did when Lucy answered for herself. Most disabled people have been on the receiving end of many mistakes, and what matters to them is usually not the mistake itself but whether the person notices and changes. A long apology, or a show of embarrassment, puts the disabled person in the position of reassuring you, which is more work for them. So does avoiding them afterwards for fear of getting it wrong again. If you are unsure what would help in future, ask simply: "Is there a better way for me to do that?" Then do it. Getting something slightly wrong while treating someone as an equal is far better than getting everything right while treating them as fragile.

It also helps to notice whether you have started avoiding someone after a mistake, and to stop.

Most disabled people have had to forgive a great many mistakes. What they remember is whether the person kept treating them as an equal.

questions.q: How can I tell what someone with facial paralysis or Parkinson's is feeling?
questions.a:
Listen to their words, their tone, their posture and what they do, rather than relying on their face, and ask when you are unsure. Bogart, Tickle-Degnen and Ambady found that observers read people with more severe facial paralysis as less happy, whatever they were actually describing, which means that the face can mislead you badly. People with Parkinson's, as Geoff's case shows, may have reduced facial expression and a flat voice while feeling as much as anyone. Read each person against their own baseline: once you know how they usually look and sound, changes become meaningful again. Many people with these conditions use words more deliberately to show feeling, so take what they say at face value. If they tell you they are delighted, they are.

And if you are the one with the still face, telling people early, as Tom did for his father, can save hours of misreading.

watch.title: How to guide a blind or partially sighted person
watch.notice: A demonstration of sighted guiding. Watch how the guide offers an arm rather than taking one, where the guided person holds, and how doorways, steps and narrow spaces are signalled through the arm and in words.

watch.title: Four awkward things to avoid saying when you meet a disabled person
watch.notice: Disabled people talk through common awkward moments with strangers. As you watch, notice how much of the awkwardness comes from well-meant assumptions, and how simple the fixes are.

watch.title: CODA: Official Trailer
watch.notice: A hearing teenager in a Deaf family. Watch how the family get each other's attention, how steadily they hold eye contact while signing, and how much of the meaning sits in their faces.
